Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Mark Zuckerberg, chief executive officer of Meta. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images First Thing newsletter US news First Thing: Meta’s treatment of children on social media in spotlight as landmark trial set to begin Several US states have accused Instagram and Facebook’s parent company of deliberately causing young people harm with its products. Plus: the Italian nuns fighting to keep control of their spot in the sun Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up here Martin Belam Tue 18 Aug 2026 07.36 EDT Last modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 07.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. More than half of the states in the US have joined together in an unprecedented lawsuit against Meta that goes to trial on Tuesday, accusing the parent company of Instagram and Facebook of deliberately designing addictive products that lured in young people and caused them harm. The sweeping legal proceedings could have profound consequences for the company. The attorneys general say that if Meta is found liable, damages could be as high as $200bn – equivalent to the company’s 2025 annual revenue. The lawmakers are also asking that Meta be compelled to change the design of its products to make them safer for children, which may have longer-term effects than a fine. What is Meta accused of? The 233-page lawsuit, first filed in October 2023, alleges that Meta regularly collects data on children under the age of 13 without parental permission. The lawmakers claim in court documents that Meta “refuses to abandon its use of known harmful features” and that its motives are based solely on profit. How has Meta responded? Meta denies all allegations and says: “Rather than sticking to the facts or the law, the states have instead decided to chase an outlandish payout. The state AGs may call this a landmark case, but their limited claims are unsubstantiated and their financial demands are vastly disproportionate.” Trump dismisses USS Lincoln criticism and snaps at CNN reporter to ‘be quiet’ View image in fullscreen Donald Trump in the Oval Office of the White House. Photograph: Samuel Corum/PI/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock Donald Trump claimed he had third-hand reports that the USS Abraham Lincoln is “beautifully maintained” despite extensive accounts of deteriorating living conditions during its lengthy deployment in the strait of Hormuz. The Navy Times and Stars and Stripes – the latter notably under increased control of the Pentagon as a defense publication – have largely confirmed reports of the Lincoln’s conditions. The publications described shortages of supplies and water and plumbing problems. Several sailors have attempted to leap from the ship according to their reports, prompting Democratic lawmakers to demand answers from the Pentagon. At the White House the president berated CNN reporter Kristen Holmes insisting that she “be quiet” and describing the reporting as fake news. The White House also attacked Holmes in social media posts , calling her “callous and vindictive”. Why have conditions on board the ship become contentious? The Lincoln, a nuclear-powered aircraft carrier left port from San Diego on 21 November 2025 and has now set a modern record for the longest time at sea without a port call. It has been more than 250 days since it has touched land. What else is causing concern with US navy ships? A US guided-missile destroyer reportedly spent four days adrift and without power in the South China Sea in July. The USS Benfold was reported to have been towed to Subic Bay in the Philippines. South Korea president calls for military independence in wake of Trump call to cut joint drills View image in fullscreen South Korea’s military carry out a drill. Photograph: Yonhap Handout/EPA South Korea’s president ⁠has renewed his push to regain independent control of the military from the US in the event of war and urged faster progress in acquiring nuclear-powered submarines after Donald Trump’s order to cut joint drills. Lee Jae Myung said on Tuesday that Seoul should ​proceed without disruption with ‌the planned transfer, during his term, of ‌wartime operational control of South Korean forces from the US – a goal he and the government have long held. Why does the US have operational control of South Korea’s forces? The issue dates back to the Korean war, which ended without a formal peace treaty in 1953, meaning the two Koreas remain technically at war. The authority to direct South Korean forces if fighting resumes still rests with the US. Seoul regained peacetime control of its own military in 1994, but wartime authority has become a potent symbol of national sovereignty. Luigi Mangione New York murder trial postponed after guilty plea in federal case View image in fullscreen Luigi Mangione appears at the Manhattan supreme court. Photograph: Jeenah Moon/Reuters A New York state ⁠judge ⁠ effectively ​postponed Luigi Mangione’s trial on murder and weapons charges over ⁠the 2024 killing of a health insurance company CEO, after Mangione pleaded ⁠guilty last week to separate federal charges. The ​trial had ‌previously been ‌scheduled to begin on 8 September. Mangione ‌has pleaded not guilty to the state charges. Mangione’s lawyers on Friday asked New York state justice Gregory Carro ‌to dismiss the charges. They argued that Mangione should not have to ​be punished for the same conduct twice. In other news … View image in fullscreen A drone photo of an election billboard by Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party in Tel Aviv. Photograph: Amir Cohen/Reuters Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s party has compared the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani , to the leaders of Iran and Hezbollah on a campaign billboard in Tel Aviv which says “They want Netanyahu to lose, don’t let them win”. Donald Trump voted by mail in Florida’s Republican primary despite his nationwide moves to restrict mail-in voting. Construction on a controversial US-Mexico border project in Big Bend national park has halted , the Trump administration said. News of construction in Texas’s largest and most-visited national park had sparked concern from environmental groups. Democratic senator Jon Ossoff has attacked Donald Trump’s “uniquely despicable” handling of the US-Israel war on Iran , accusing the US president of “re-rigging” a corrupt system for himself . Stat of the day: Tens of thousands pay tribute to Jason Arday at Trafalgar Square vigil View image in fullscreen People gather for a memorial event at Trafalgar Square for the academic Jason Arday. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images An estimated 30,000 mourners gathered in London for a vigil honoring Jason Arday . Friends, campaigners, and lawmakers paid tribute to the 41-year-old former Cambridge professor, who was pronounced dead on Friday. He had recently resigned his sociology of education post following disputed allegations of plagiarism and career inaccuracies . Culture Pick: Hollywood continues to fail child stars and Hayden Panettiere is the latest casualty View image in fullscreen Hayden Panettiere in 2007. Photograph: Matt Sayles/AP Jesse Hassenger writes that the untimely death of the Heroes and Scream star was a tragic ending to a life filled with darkness in an industry that still lets its younger stars down. Don’t miss this: Visual effects maestro Rick Baker on a monstrously good career View image in fullscreen Rick Baker Photograph: Courtesy Locarno Film Festival Rick Baker helped define Hollywood’s creature features with his wild makeup effects skills. Here he talks about Gremlins, his love of simians – and why AI will never replace expert design. … or this: What we know about Tupac Shakur’s death and what to expect from murder trial View image in fullscreen Tupac Shakur. Photograph: Ron Galella/Ron Galella Collection/Getty Images Nearly 30 years after Tupac Shakur was killed in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas, the only man ever charged in connection with the rapper’s death is now on trial. Here is what we can expect . Climate check: Extreme heat more dangerous for people 60 and over than previously thought View image in fullscreen Seniors playing in Maximo Gomez Park, Florida. Photograph: Jeff Greenberg/Jeffrey Greenberg/UCG/Universal Images Group/Getty Images Older adults will bear the brunt of increasingly frequent sustained spells of extreme heat globally. Research has found that people aged 60 and over face dangers to their health from exposure to heat at much lower temperatures than previously thought . Last Thing: Nuns fight Italian town’s plans to take away their beach club View image in fullscreen Crowded sandy beach in Spotorno, Italy. Photograph: aerial-photos.com/Alamy A group of Italian nuns is fighting local council plans to take their beach club away from them . The nuns have been managing the resort since 1946. https://www.dw.com/en/author-or-artifici.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5O4R8 The pavilion of the Guest of Honor, the Czech Republic, at the 2026 Frankfurt Book Fair Image: Hannes P. Albert/AFP Advertisement It's the hot-button topic at the Frankfurt Book Fair : How profoundly will artificial intelligence (AI) transform the book industry, and how can this transformation be regulated? Given the warnings about the technology's long-term risks to humanity as a whole, such debates might appear rather narrow in scope. In reality, however, they concern very concrete issues — copyright protection, the power of tech giants and the future of creativity. Many agree that the political measures taken don't go far enough. This year, however, another aspect has entered the debate: Can we actually recognize when a text has been written with the help of artificial intelligence, and if so, can this be proven? These are some of the questions raised by the current scandal surrounding Haitian-Canadian author Thelyson Orelien and his debut novel, "C'etait ca ou mourir," (This title means "It Was Either That or Die" in English but an English translation has not yet been published), which was published in Canada in the spring. The controversy around Thelyson Orelien's book has sparked a larger debate on AI and authorship Image: Joel Saget/AFP/dpa/picture alliance The book about global migration was universally acclaimed, with translation rights sold in more than 20 languages. Soon after the book was published in France, it was longlisted for the prestigious Prix Goncourt. But then, all of a sudden, allegations emerged that the book had been written almost entirely using AI. Orelien, a rising literary star, found himself branded a fraud despite denying all the allegations. His nomination for the Goncourt was withdrawn. So, who should we believe? An author or an AI that claims to have identified AI-generated writing? When the origins of texts become uncertain "We will have to learn to live with doubt," says Hannes Bajohr, a professor of German literature at the University of California, Berkeley. Hannes Bajohr, professor for German Studies at the University of California, Berkeley Image: Jen Siska He has spent years examining how AI is changing both writing and reading. His prediction: If the origins of texts can no longer be reliably established, we will have to evaluate them differently. What matters will be their quality alone, rather than whether AI was used in the writing process. Nina George, a best-selling author and the honorary president of the European Writers' Council, is unwilling to accept this. At the Frankfurt Book Fair, she was awarded the Friedrich Perthes Prize in recognition of her commitment to issues such as AI and copyright reform. Nina George is a leading advocate for European authors' rights and copyright reform Image: Sabine Kieselbach/DW George has addressed the European Parliament and the German Bundestag, speaking and writing tirelessly about the dangers of AI models. It is perverse, she says, that an author should suddenly have to prove that their writing is the creation of a human. The focus of her campaigns are the tech corporations' self-serving mentality and copyright protection. Can anyone become an author with AI? But what if an author sees AI not as an enemy but as a tool that makes writing easier? US author and artist Luke Stoffel deliberately used AI in his memoir, "How To Win One Million Dollars and Shit Glitter," and was open about doing so. "I'm dyslexic," he said in a video interview. "I've always written and made up stories, but I never dared to take them any further." Luke Stoffel talks openly about his use of AI when writing Image: Privat It was only with the help of AI, he said, that he was able to fulfill his dream. The technology drew his attention to weaknesses in his writing and suggested a marketing strategy that actually worked. In May 2026, he received an award from the Independent Book Publishers Association (IBPA) for the book. For South African author Coral Hart, AI is actually the foundation of her business model. Publishing under various pseudonyms, each year she releases more than 200 different novels, spanning the genres of romance, thriller and mystery. She sees herself as an ideas person, as well as an editor and publisher. Although none of her books has yet become a bestseller, the business is profitable, she says, and each book reaches more than 5,000 people according to her. Many publishers already working with AI Stoffel considers the entire debate hypocritical and points out that many publishers have been working with AI tools for some time. He's certain that "right now, a million-copy bestseller is being printed that was created with the help of AI. The author won't admit it, and then there'll be a scandal." It is entirely possible that the scandal surrounding Thelyson Orelien is precisely that story. But we may never know for sure. For now, the battle against the tech giants continues, some of which are themselves increasingly concerned about losing control. At the very start of the Frankfurt fair, the German Publishers and Booksellers Association issued an appeal to policymakers in Berlin and Brussels, calling for stricter regulation of artificial intelligence, which they said is more urgent than ever. More than 140 publishers have signed it. But for now, it remains just an appeal. And the question of what authors themselves should be permitted to do with AI will undoubtedly continue to fuel debates in the future. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Ethiopian forces took control of Tigray's main city Mekelle from rebel forces last week By Hafsa Khalil Â and Â Kaleb Moges ,Â BBC Africa Published 9 October 2026 Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of an "all-out invasion" of its northern Tigray region and warned it will defend itself, days after residents told the BBC Eritrean troops had crossed into the country. In a letter sent to the UN Security Council and seen by the BBC, Ethiopia's foreign minister called it a "blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia's inherent right to self-defence". Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel responded by saying it was facing "an unprovoked war of aggression" from its neighbour. Fighting broke out two weeks ago between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). Both blame each other for violating a 2022 deal that ended a civil war. Ethiopia says Eritrea is backing the TPLF, which it denies. During the two-year civil war, Eritrea was a key ally of the Ethiopian government, having fought alongside them against the TPLF. But relations between the two neighbours have since deteriorated - largely over the Ethiopian prime minister's ambition to take ownership of one of Eritrea's Red Sea ports - leading to the severing of diplomatic ties last week. Accusing Eritrea of violating its sovereignty, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said Eritrean forces had advanced up to 60km (37 miles) into Tigray. Ethiopian drone strikes reportedly targeted Eritrean forces in the Tigrayan town of Adigrat on Wednesday and Thursday, amid fears of a wider regional war. US-based conflict monitor Acled said "Eritrean troops and ammunition" in Adigrat were hit by "multiple drone strikes" overnight. One resident told AFP news agency "there were many, many drone strikes", and that some Eritrean lorries had been destroyed. Another witness said Eritrean forces appeared to be retreating north after the strikes, AFP reported. There have so far been no verified reports of casualties. The BBC is unable to report from Tigray. Dated 8 October, Ethiopia's letter to UN Security Council members read: "In this time of difficulty, when Ethiopia is left with no other option but to defend itself, we count on your understanding, support, and solidarity." But while Ethiopia accuses its neighbour of supporting the TPLF, Eritrea has blamed the conflict on Ethiopia's leaders, and accused them looking for a reason to seize Eritrean territory. On Friday, Eritrea's information minister called the accusations levelled against Asmara as "duplicity in their most extreme forms". In a post on X, he said Ethiopia was "openly working to bring about regime change in Eritrea by providing shelter and support to certain mercenaries who claim to be opposition". Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, but ties were only normalised in 2018, when Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power. This latest unrest follows months of tension and the launch of new alliance of armed groups in Ethiopia - including the TPLF - in September. Last week, TPLF forces withdrew from Tigray's main city of Mekelle, which is 115km (71 miles) south of Adigrat and is now under army control. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6pv.text: Image source, Getty Images By Tinshui Yeung Published 11 October 2026 Donald Trump has claimed that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire", with Kyiv saying it would support such a move but Moscow yet to comment. The US president insisted that it was "effective immediately" but provided no details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky initially expressed surprise at the announcement, before saying Kyiv would support it if Moscow did. He also accused Russia of striking Ukrainian energy facilities after Trump's post. Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to curtailing revenue for Moscow's war machine - so Russia can fulfil a recently-struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market. The diesel deal, temporarily undoing sanctions on Russian imports, is attracting growing criticism. Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin. European officials and some US politicians, including from Trump's Republican party, have said they do not support it. The deal is Trump's latest effort to lower domestic fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections, having spent months grappling with the political consequences of the war with Iran which has pushed up global fuel prices, particularly those for diesel. That has soured Trump's standing with the American public, who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation. Figure caption, Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim? Zelensky said it was "news" to him that an energy truce was in effect in comments to news site Axios, before writing on social media that his officials "look forward to clear details of America's dialogue with Russia". "Ukraine is ready not to strike at Russian energy and we count on Russia's similar readiness and on the agreement of the president of the United States of America on this," he said. The BBC has asked the White House for further details. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support. Zelensky later said Russia had hit a power plant in Kyiv with a drone, causing power cuts, followed by strikes on energy facilities in the north-eastern Kharkiv region. "All of this happened after the president of the United States made his statement about an energy ceasefire," he said. For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure. Moscow said the installations it hits were legitimate targets because they supported Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war". The attacks have disrupted energy supplies on both sides. Image source, Telegram/Crimeanwind Image caption, Huge plumes of smoke seen rising in the skies from the site where the Slavneft-Yanos oil refinery in Russia is located on 6 August Earlier on Sunday, UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC that the UK did not support it , while EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas echoed Zelensky's criticism of it on Saturday. The deal has also attracted criticism from politicians of both main US parties. Seven senators, including three Democrats and four Republicans, have published a statement saying Trump's deal "runs directly counter" to a law that had explicitly banned Russian energy imports. "Congress was clear: the US should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our Nato Allies," they said, urging the Trump administration to "reverse course". Republican Senator Thom Tillis, one of the seven, told NBC News that the deal "absolutely will" put American lives at risk. On Saturday Trump accused Zelensky of wanting to "make problems for the world" by continuing to authorise attacks on Russian refineries following the Ukrainian leader's criticism of the diesel deal. The US president suggested that it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president". Zelensky pledged to hold elections - despite them being suspended by the Ukrainian constitution during wartime - if Russia agreed to a 60-day total ceasefire. The Ukrainian president previously resisted calls from the US for fresh elections, pointing to complications with holding a vote in parts of the country that are active war zones or under Russian occupation. Trump, however, has repeatedly accused the Ukrainian leader of using the war to stay in power. Meanwhile, strikes and fighting on the ground continue in the four-year-long war. Six people were killed in attacks on two Ukrainian cities on Sunday, regional officials said. One person was killed in Russia's Belgorod region, which borders Ukraine, while another man was killed in a drone attack in the Russian-occupied Donetsk region, officials said. https://www.irishtimes.com/world/europe/.text: Europe Biljana Plavsic, the only woman charged with war crimes in the Balkan wars, dies aged 96 Known as the Iron Lady of the Balkans, she expressed remorse after pleading guilty but later recanted Former Bosnian Serb president Biljana Plavsic at her sentencing hearing at the War Crimes Tribunal on December 16th, 2002 in The Hague, Netherlands. Photograph: Michel Porro/Getty Images) Andrew Higgins Sun Oct 04 2026 - 22:46 • 7 MIN READ Biljana Plavsic, a Bosnian Serb biologist and ultra-nationalist political leader during the Balkan wars of the 1990s, has died in Serbia ’s capital, Belgrade, aged 96. She pleaded guilty to one count of crimes against humanity and expressed remorse, but later recanted, saying she “would do the same again”. Her death was announced on Thursday by Serbian state media. No other details were provided. Plavsic, a former professor at Sarajevo University who studied in Zagreb, Croatia , New York, London and Prague, and wrote more than 100 scientific papers, became notorious in the 1990s for applying biology to politics when the multi-ethnic state of Yugoslavia disintegrated. She declared Bosnia’s Muslim population “deformed genetic material” and railed against mixed marriages, common before the war, as leading to “the degeneration of Serb nationality”. Often coldly indifferent to the suffering of non-Serbs, she was known as the Iron Lady of the Balkans, a nickname inspired by Soviet descriptions of Britain’s Margaret Thatcher . But the name Plavsic relished most was a tribute that Serb fighters daubed on the side of their tanks: Empress. READ MORE Welcome to the new Global Briefing newsletter ‘Where is his authority?’ Germany is losing patience with Friedrich Merz After my friend lost his job, he asked AI what came next Raphaël Glucksmann’s refusal to use the word ‘genocide’ divides France’s left “She was educated, a professor but a real hard-line nationalist,” recalled Laura Silber, co-author of The Death of Yugoslavia, who interviewed Plavsic several times during the 1992-95 war in Bosnia. “She was prim and proper – school marmish in demeanour – so it was especially shocking to hear the ugly nationalist rhetoric coming out of her mouth.” Olivera Simic, an Australian scholar from Bosnia who interviewed Plavsic for hundreds of hours in her later years, remembered her as highly intelligent but often blind to the suffering of non-Serbs. “She was not a monster and would express from time to time that she felt sorry for everyone – and then quickly start talking about Serb victims and cry over them,” Simic said in a telephone interview. For nearly four years, Plavsic served as vice president of Republika Srpska, a Serb enclave in Bosnia that declared itself a separate state in 1992 and began a programme aimed at driving out Muslims, Croats and other non-Serb residents. In that role, she worked closely with Radovan Karadzic, the self-declared state’s president, who in 2016 was convicted of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity by a United Nations tribunal. She rejected the term “ethnic cleansing” in her interviews with Simic, a law professor at Griffith University in Australia, describing the separation of different peoples as a “natural process.” According to Simic, Plavsic believed that “everyone should live with their own tribe” and, as a result, “willingly turned a blind eye” to the suffering this caused when ethnic groups were separated at gunpoint “because she was only interested in protecting her own tribe.” Testifying as a witness at The Hague trial of Serbia’s wartime leader Slobodan Milosevic, Vojislav Seselj, the founder of a far-right Serb political party who was also charged with war crimes, said that Plavsic “held very extremist positions during the war, insufferably extremist, even for me, and they bothered even me as a declared Serb nationalist.” After the war ended, Plavsic muted her anti-Muslim fervour, broke with Karadzic, accusing him of corruption, and in 1996 took over as president of Republika Srpska with support from the West, which viewed her as a partner for peace. She was for a time hailed as a symbol of reconciliation after she expressed remorse during a 2002 sentencing hearing in The Hague. “I have now come to the belief and accept the fact that many thousands of innocent people were the victims of an organised, systematic effort to remove Muslims and Croats from the territory claimed by Serbs,” she said. Serbs, driven by “an obsession to never become victims,” had “allowed ourselves to become victimisers,” she told the court. Plavsic was the only woman among more than 150 people indicted by the international court for war crimes in former Yugoslavia. In 2003, she received an 11-year sentence for persecution, a crime against humanity, as part of a plea bargain that allowed her to avoid a trial on charges of complicity in genocide. In contrast with Karadzic, who went into hiding for more than a decade and, after his arrest, boycotted parts of his trial in The Hague, Plavsic surrendered voluntarily and cooperated with the tribunal. After initially pleading not guilty, she later pleaded guilty on one count, acknowledging that Serb forces had committed crimes and her own responsibility for these. “The knowledge that I am responsible for such human suffering and for soiling the character of my people will always be with me,” she told the court. The judge said that Plavsic had not conceived or planned the violent Serbian campaign of ethnic separation that killed tens of thousands of Muslims and Croats and expelled many more from their lands with “great brutality,” but that she had embraced, supported and contributed to it. “This is a crime of utmost gravity,” he said. Victims of the war and some human rights groups criticised her sentence as too lenient. But others said the major issue in Plavsic’s confession and guilty plea was that they would make denials by other Serbian leaders more difficult. “In a region where denial and revisionism are central and where the tribunal is seen with scepticism, Ms. Plavsic’s gesture is striking,” Alex Boraine, a member of South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission, told the court. Fellow Serb nationalists, appalled by the confession in The Hague, denounced her as a traitor for deviating from the narrative that Serbs were innocent victims. They embraced her as a hero when she later recanted and declared herself and Serbs blameless. The grip that the narrative of innocence still holds on many Serbs was on ghoulish display in September when thousands, including Serbian government ministers and the son of President Aleksandar Vucic, turned out in Belgrade for the funeral of Ratko Mladic, a Bosnian Serb general convicted of genocide and known as the Butcher of Bosnia. Plavsic’s contrition, if ever more than a ploy to avoid a lengthy trial and escape genocide charges, did not last long. Released early from prison in 2009 for good behaviour, she settled in Belgrade and quickly retreated from what Simic, author of the 2025 book “Madam War Criminal,” concluded was “fake remorse” in The Hague. Divorced with no children, she lived alone in a modest Belgrade apartment decorated with Orthodox Christian icons and a wooden cross made for her by a fellow inmate convicted of genocide for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre. “She believes she sacrificed herself for ‘her people’ and did not show any ability to critically reflect on her actions but persistently justified and rationalised her behaviour, which she always perceived as highly ethical, moral and legitimate,” Simic wrote in her book. “She told me on many occasions during our conversations that if the circumstances would arise again she would most likely respond the same way.” The debate rages in former Yugoslavia, where the 1995 massacre of Bosniaks at Srebrenica has been legally recognised as genocide but atrocities committed by Serb forces against Croats in Vukovar in 1991 and by Croats against Bosniaks in Mostar during a 1993-94 siege have been classified as war crimes and crimes against humanity. Biljana Plavsic was born on July 7th, 1930, in Tuzla, then part of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. She grew up in Sarajevo, to which her affluent family moved when she was four. Her father was a prominent scientist who had been educated in Vienna, and she was raised on books and stories celebrating an infamous relative — Gavrilo Princip, a Serb nationalist who precipitated the first World War in 1914 by assassinating Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, in Sarajevo. Eleven years old when Nazi Germany invaded Bosnia in 1941, she witnessed Serbs being executed in the street and lost dozens of relatives to brutal ethnic purges carried out by the Ustashe, a Croatian fascist group that led the Independent State of Croatia, a puppet state of Germany formed during the second World War. After the defeat of the Nazis, Bosnia became one of six republics in the newly declared Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Despite her family’s hostility to communism, Plavsic, who never joined the party, embarked on a highly successful academic career focused on plant virology. This included two years of botany research in the 1970s at Cornell University. A popular biology professor in Sarajevo, she had a reputation as an exacting but fair-minded scholar who held all students, no matter their ethnicity, to the same high standards. Elected dean of Sarajevo University’s faculty of natural sciences and mathematics in 1987, she turned to politics in 1990 when she became the Serb member of a collective, multiethnic presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then still part of Yugoslavia. When Slovenia and Croatia, two other Yugoslav republics, broke away to declare independence in 1991, Bosniaks began demanding their own state, too — a prospect that terrified Plavsic and many other Serbs. In interviews with Simic, the Australia-based scholar, before her death, Plavsic often referred to 1991 as “the continuation of 1941,” a replay of the World War II conflict between Nazi-aligned Croats and anti-fascist Serbs that, she believed, “never finished.” She told Simic years later in Belgrade that everything she did was motivated by a desire to avoid “the extinction of the Serb people.” Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats all suffered and, Simic said, Plavsic’s obsession with crimes against her own people was part of a bigger problem across former Yugoslavia. “Everyone talks about their own victims, never their own perpetrators — no one,” Simic said. “This is the problem. Everyone wants to talk about their victimhood, never their perpetrators. They think nobody acknowledges crimes done against them, no matter how big or small.” - This article originally appeared in The New York Times .
